items.title: 2026 AI100 Report Released: (AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI; New From Stanford )
items.raw_text: From a Stanford University Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI) Post/Summary: The One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence , known as AI100, released its third report, painting a striking picture of a technology transforming nearly every corner of human society faster than anyone anticipated. Launched in 2014 with an endowment from Eric and Mary Horvitz, AI100 is a longitudinal project led by an international Standing Committee of AI experts, currently chaired by Sheila McIlraith of the University of Toronto, and administered out of Stanford HAI. Every five years, the Standing Committee commissions a study that brings together researchers to assess AI’s advances and their effects on society. The 2026 study panel, led by Michael Wooldridge of the University of Oxford, draws on disciplines including computer science, philosophy, and sociology. The latest report offers a sweeping look at where AI stands today and where it may be headed. [Clip] Science Is Being Transformed AI is compressing scientific timescales dramatically, shrinking research timelines from years to months or even weeks. Within a decade, AI-powered laboratories are expected to become the norm across scientific disciplines. But the report warns that validating machine-generated discoveries will require rigorous new methods, and that the broader influence of AI on human behavior, culture, and collective decision-making demands urgent scientific attention. items.title: Exploring the World’s Languages with Language Explorer (New Research Tool From Google Research)
items.raw_text: From a Google Research Blog Post: Building products that reflect the world’s linguistic diversity takes far more than software engineering; it requires close collaboration with the communities we aim to serve, building in a way that’s deeply aligned and respectful of local communities, heritage, history, values and context. [Clip] But gathering this data is only one part of the journey. Preserving language vitality requires working closely with native speakers, academic institutions, and cultural organizations. Partnerships, such as our coalition with the Gates Foundation , ensure that modern digital tools reflect the nuances and authentic voices of their communities. Expanding language coverage responsibly also requires deeply understanding linguistic diversity on a global scale. This approach enables products like Gboard , our Android keyboard, to support 900+ language varieties. To better appreciate the breadth and complexity of this speech diversity, we’ve been working on a tool to help visualize the world’s linguistic diversity, inspired by earlier visualization initiatives like Google Earth . The Language Explorer is an interactive web platform designed to let researchers, educators, and language enthusiasts discover and visualize linguistic diversity around the world. Developed as part of our 1,000 Languages Initiative , the Language Explorer brings together data across thousands of languages, building on our open-source LinguaMeta dataset . items.title: CBC Report: University Libraries are Being Swarmed by AI Bots, Putting Public Access at Risk
items.raw_text: From the CBC: University libraries say entire collections are being knocked offline by persistent streams of unruly bots trying to access their archives, which include academic, historical and government documents. “They’re just out there on the internet, just bombarding us with trying to grab up as much material as possible,” Jill Strykowski, cataloguing and government documents lead at San Jose State University, told CBC News. Eric Hellman, executive director of Project Gutenberg — a U.S.-based volunteer organization that digitizes and archives cultural works and distributes eBooks — wrote in a blog last year that these bots, which he characterizes as poorly programmed “monstrosities,” are “destroying open access” on the internet. He tells CBC News that “everything’s gotten worse” since he wrote that. [Clip] Some libraries have set up CAPTCHA challenges or other verification systems to weed out bots. The problem is, those measures can also weed out the good bots, says Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative academic initiative at NYU Law School and the University of Warwick focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions. Some libraries have also begun to require login credentials, a controversial move that those who spoke to CBC News say they want to avoid because it puts barriers on human access. While researchers are increasingly integrating AI into their research journeys, a recent survey conducted by OUP shows their trust in AI outputs remains low. items.title: Big Ideas, Small Budgets: The November/December Issue of Public Libraries is Here
items.raw_text: The November/December 2026 issue of Public Libraries is now available. In Big Ideas, Small Budgets, we explore what innovation looks like in the day-to-day work of public libraries, from making a space more welcoming to connecting patrons with services they need. Inside this issue Elevated Library Design on Any Budget — Interior designer Meghan Bentheimer shares ways to make library spaces more welcoming and functional, with advice on where to focus your budget. (Not) Closing the Books — Anthony Aycock looks at how partnerships with legal experts can expand access to legal information and assistance. Small Grants, Big Impact — Justin Dyer explores how libraries use microgrants and community partnerships to bring new ideas to life. Also in this issue, Aimee Adams looks beyond the familiar 1,000 Books Before Kindergarten model, Catherine Hakala-Ausperk explores how library spaces can encourage play and creativity, and Sara Goek highlights resources for building digital literacy. In The Big Idea , Gretchen Kaser Corsillo makes the case for sustained investment in public libraries. PLA members and subscribers can read the November/December issue of Public Libraries . items.title: Libraries Shaping AI Together
items.raw_text: When a group of Pottsboro, TX residents sat down at the library and asked ChatGPT, “Where can I send a fax in Pottsboro?” we hoped it would suggest the library. Instead, it told them to drive twelve miles to a mail store in another town. The question was part of a library workshop where residents tested what AI tools know, and don’t know, about our town. We expected that it might not know everything locals know. We did not expect it to send people to other towns to find services and activities available here. Being a tourist destination, it would be helpful for responses to include local restaurants, hotels, and fishing guides. That moment was on my mind when I went to Washington, DC, for the AI Civics convening hosted by Data & Society. AI Civics treats AI as part of civic life, something communities have a right to shape, not just a tool to learn. Our cohort is a mix of big city library systems, small town libraries like ours, and the National Digital Inclusion Alliance. Each of us is running our own pilot. Different Libraries, Same Questions It turns out a library serving a few hundred people and one serving tens of thousands have a lot in common. We keep running into the same questions. Who gets represented in AI? Who gets left out? Who gets a say? And there is no customer service number you can call to fix what ChatGPT says about your town. items.title: Scaffolding Early Literacy Learning During Public Library Storytime
items.raw_text: Public library storytimes are more than just a fun time for children; beneath the read-alouds, singing songs, fingerplays, bubbles, and movement activities, storytimes are packed with abundant opportunities that support children’s literacy learning [1]. We all know intentionality is a key ingredient to promote learning in storytime [2]. One way to do this is by incorporating the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) [3], an educational theory by Lev Vygotsky, into storytime planning and design. With a little bit of foreplanning, we can structure literacy experiences to align with children’s developmental levels—the perfect spot for learning—neither too easy nor too challenging. This article provides an introduction and practical tips for storytime providers on how to intentionally scaffold learning during picture book reading in storytime using the ZPD. The Zone of Proximal Development So what exactly is the Zone of Proximal Development? The ZPD, as explained by Vygotsky, is the gap between what children can do alone and what children can do with the guidance of more knowledgeable others (Vygotsky et al., 1978). Think of it as a linear continuum. There are three different learning levels. Imagine that at one end of the continuum is a task children can perform independently. At the other end of the continuum is a task children cannot perform, even with help. And in the middle of the continuum is the ZPD, in which children can perform the task with guidance and support. items.title: Erica Kent On The Light And Shadows Of Her Magnificent New Novel
items.raw_text: Reader’s first meet Jessica Ryder, the captivating protagonist of Erica Kent’s Black Dog , as a smart and brash eleven-year-old living with her alcoholic father in Brookline, Massachusetts. It’s 1980 and Jessica, an ardent music fan, is devastated over the death of John Lennon. In a misguided attempt to comfort her, Jessica’s father offers her a beer. This fateful act kicks off a near-decade long struggle with alcohol and drugs, which Kent depicts with clarity and empathy. Kent masterfully charts Jessica’s adolescence as the young woman negotiates her complicated family dynamic, not only with her father, but also with her mother and sister, who live in a far different socioeconomic world in nearby Boston. What follows is not only a riveting coming of age story but also a clear-eyed examination of the often fraught road to recovery. The reviews have been rapturous for Black Dog . Library Journal wrote, “Kent demonstrates her skills with evocative and atmospheric prose” and Pulitzer-Prize winner Richard Russo raved, “Erica Kent’s Black Dog takes the reader on a truly terrifying journey, but guess what? I’m so, so glad I fastened my seatbelt, gritted my teeth, and climbed aboard.” Kent spoke with us about using her setting as a character, capturing Jessica’s voice, and allowing the story to find her. items.title: “Let’s Get Weird” – Beck Kubrick on Their Chilling New Graphic Novel
items.raw_text: Despite growing up in the bucolic New England town of Clossdale, Ash Hargreeves lives under a shadow of suspicion. When Ash was a baby, her mother died a fiery death soon after police discovered she was The Clossdale Killer, a serial killer whose victims were all popular high school girls. Years later, when five of Ash’s classmates disappear and townspeople discover dead bodies in the forest, all signs point to Ash as the most logical suspect. Over the course of one terrifying night, Ash teams up with her only two friends, Cassie and Jamie, to discover the real culprit, guided by their mantra WWJLCD (What Would Jamie Lee Curtis Do?). Laugh out loud funny with surprising twists, Beck Kubrick’s Dead Girls is a taut thriller that deftly upends the slasher genre. Critics have praised the graphic novel, with Kirkus Reviews hailing it as a “chilling slasher that effectively explores legacy, identity, confronting the past—and refusing to be defined by it.” We spoke to Kubrick about constructing the elaborate mysteries Dead Girls , playing with the framework of horror, and the “terrible feral” high schoolers at the heart of the story. items.title: E-Rate Under Threat: Take a Stand and Show Up for E-Rate
items.raw_text: After thirty years of keeping libraries online, the E-Rate program has seen its share of challenges. Just in the last two years, the program weathered the loss of support for hotspot lending and suffered through a Supreme Court Challenge . While the Supreme Court decision ultimately went in our favor, there is no time to sit back and relax for library advocates. In June, the Federal Communication’s Commission (FCC) launched a proceeding (officially, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking) that threatens to terminate this vital program. Now is the time to show up for E-Rate and tell the FCC what broadband access at your library means for your community. A Quick E-Rate Refresher One of four programs within the FCC’s Universal Service Fund, set up in the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the E-Rate program was established to ensure public libraries and K-12 schools have affordable access to advanced telecommunications (i.e., broadband and internet access). Today, E-Rate provides funding to almost three-quarters of public libraries to help offset monthly internet service costs and the costs for eligible technology necessary for making sure Wi-Fi is available throughout the building. How much are we talking about? Currently the program sends about $2.4 billion to public libraries and K-12 schools annually. items.title: Bringing Big Ideas Home: Reflections from PLA 2026 in Minneapolis
items.raw_text: The most valuable takeaway from my time at the Public Library Association Conference wasn’t just new ideas; it was a renewed sense of purpose. As the director of a small, rural library in Elba, Alabama, I was thrilled to receive a PLA scholarship to attend the conference in Minneapolis. PLA has supported our library in meaningful ways over the years, including a 2019 grant that funded a high school intern. That student is now about to graduate from college and, inspired by her experience at our library, is pursuing her MLS. Moments like that are a powerful reminder of the long-term impact of library work. Energy, Inspiration, and Hard Conversations I attended with a colleague from a neighboring library, and from the moment we walked into the Minneapolis Convention Center, the energy was contagious. We immediately felt welcomed, not just by the upbeat registration staff but by the shared sense of purpose among attendees. The opening session set the tone. Hearing from speakers, including Bryan Stevenson, was both inspiring and challenging. His remarks encouraged me to reflect more deeply on local history in my own community, including the possibility of researching and acknowledging difficult chapters like lynchings. I left with a desire to partner with our local historical preservation group to explore ways to honor and remember those stories. items.title: Building Acceptance and Community at PLA 2026
items.raw_text: My name is Lana Sweeting, and I was lucky enough to be selected for a 2026 PLA scholarship. I serve as an Adult Reference Librarian in Portland, Oregon, where much of my work focuses on serving the Black community through programming, collections, and outreach. While there were many sessions that were relevant and helpful to my everyday work, two in particular invigorated my work as a public librarian. First, I felt very drawn to the session “Every Story Matters, Every Body Belongs: Fat Inclusive Libraries.” The presenter, Amelia Mason, was absolutely wonderful and very knowledgeable on the subject. I was locked in from the very first slide, which simply said, “I Am Fat.” The honest and positive energy went up from there. Along with sharing quantitative data, Amelia discussed myths surrounding fatness, as well as history, race, fat acceptance and neutrality, and how these issues apply to library spaces and other spaces we regularly occupy. For example, Amelia noted that PLA shirts on the website only went up to size 3XL. After the session, I felt informed and inspired to take this information back to Multnomah County Library. The session included a resource booklist that inspired me to create a booklist and display for my own library and begin conversations around diversity audits of our catalog so we can make relevant materials more accessible. items.title: The Future Is Now: Black Men in Libraries
items.raw_text: I appreciated the chance to attend the PLA 2026 Conference. As an early-career librarian and MLIS student at the University of South Florida, I had no idea what to expect, but I am proud to report that I was not let down. I came to Minneapolis with a strong desire to learn more about public libraries, and I did just that. I learned more about how to strengthen library boards and foundations, how to protect queer and trans staff, and how to provide library services to those who are incarcerated. I am really happy with my experience. I attended various community-related sessions because it is so important to build relationships and have a sense of belonging, especially in today’s tumultuous political climate. This is also important in my Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) journey, where I promote positive connections, encourage librarians to embrace diversity, and build relationships with those around them. PLA was an amazing conference filled with experts who were welcoming and eager to answer questions from the audience. It was difficult to choose just one program to highlight because I genuinely enjoyed all the sessions. However, one stood out to me. My favorite was Black Men in Libraries: Our History, Our Heroes, and Our Horizon . items.title: ALA Launches Reporting Form for Incidents Against Immigrants in Libraries
items.raw_text: Acknowledgments: The author thanks Hayley Park of the University of Maryland for her contributions to language used in this article and Derek Wilmott of the University of Toledo for his assistance in developing the incident reporting form. Libraries across the country are navigating heightened immigration enforcement activity while trying to support community members and staff. Library leaders may face difficult decisions about how to respond to enforcement activity, address harassment, communicate with their communities, and protect patrons and employees, often with limited information about what other libraries are experiencing. Consider a public library responding to increased immigration enforcement activity in its community. Library leadership might consider issuing a public statement supporting immigrants but ultimately decide against it after consulting legal counsel, concerned that doing so could make the library a target. How can library leaders make decisions like this when much of the information available to them comes from anecdotal experiences or informal conversations with colleagues? Better data can help. The Services to Refugees, Immigrants, and Displaced Persons (SRIDP) Subcommittee is proud to announce the launch of the Incidents Against Immigrants in Libraries reporting form . items.title: Art for Everyone: How Public Libraries Expand Access
items.raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. items.title: “I Want You To Stay Up Late To Finish The Book” — Juno Dawson On Her Chilling “Survival Show”
items.raw_text: Juno Dawson’s Survival Show begins with an irresistible premise: a reality TV show where contestants vie for one of five spots in a band, where each week the lowest-ranking contestant gets executed on live television. Dawson centers the book around Taryn Beck, a gutsy seventeen-year-old who’s survived a climate disaster and war and now lives in a refugee camp with her father and critically ill brother. When Taryn lands a chance to audition for Starmaker , the television show that has become a global phenomenon and launched past winners to superstardom, it seems like the best opportunity for her to provide her brother with desperately needed medical care. Yet when she begins rehearsing with her fellow contestants, Taryn must confront the challenge of collaborating and competing with contestants whose success could mean her death. Intrigue and romance quickly follow, and Dawson balances the gloom of her dystopian setting with a dark wit. Dawson previous books include This Book Is Gay and Clean, and critics have heaped similar praise on Survival Show . In their starred reviews, Publishers Weekly wrote, “This chilling, satirical dystopian adventure defies expectations,” and Kirkus stated, “Fast-paced and heart-wrenchingly suspenseful, this work combines the glitter, drama, and cutthroat competition of the pop music industry with the looming threat of death.” Author photo courtesy of Eivind Hansen. items.title: Autism Acceptance at All Ages
items.raw_text: Autism acceptance efforts have come a long way in recent years, and libraries are one of the key reasons why. As a librarian and the mother of two sons with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), I’ve witnessed this progress firsthand. In my capacity as the assistant director of the Beals Memorial Library (BML), I’ve seen how efforts to create more inclusive programs, services, and spaces can promote positive social change that dra-matically improves people’s quality of life, disabled or not. Through our “See Beyond the Spectrum” initiative, in recent years, BML has established new ASD-friendly programs, made our existing programs more accessible, updated our collections with texts by autistic writers, and established an autism caregiver support group. Our staff have gone through autism awareness training, and we’ve established partnerships with local organizations that serve autistic youth. Much of this workhas been supported by external grants, including generous funding from the ALA’s “Libraries Transforming Communities” initiative, which seeks to help libraries become more accessible to patrons with disabilities. Everything we’ve done has proved beneficial, both inside and outside of the library. Staff-patron interactions are more productive and less awkward. Families feel welcomed, and patrons with ASD feel comfortable being themselves when they visit. Community members are more knowledgeable about ASD and are actively talking about it. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: Advocacy at the Heart of Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Public libraries face no shortage of challenges today. Ongoing censorship efforts, increasing threats to staff safety, growing public distrust of institutions, and rapid technological change continue to reshape the work of libraries and the people who sustain them. In this environment, advocacy matters more than ever. That message came through clearly at the 2026 Public Library Association conference, where many sessions focused on helping librarians strengthen their advocacy skills. At the heart of every library are the workers who understand its value best and are often its strongest advocates. One session I attended, “Advocacy at the Core of ALA’s Next 150 Years,” featured Sam Helmick, Maria McCauley, Daniel Montgomery, and Lisa Varga. The panel offered practical strategies for advocacy, including using easy digital tools to contact legislators, participating in National Library Legislative Day, supporting legislation such as the Right to Read Act, and inviting elected officials into library spaces to see the work firsthand. Another standout session, “Advocacy Strategies for Getting Things Done,” featured Lisa Wells, Amanda Kordeliski, Tim Miller, Gail Oehler, and Kelly Sitzman from libraries across Oklahoma. Their discussion focused on the power of quiet advocacy. Quiet advocacy means building relationships with legislators before you urgently need their support. items.title: Creating Meaningful Connections Through Memory Cafés
items.raw_text: The 2026 Public Library Association conference featured many excellent sessions focused on programming and community engagement, but one that especially resonated with me was “Memory Cafés in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections,” presented by Christina M. Johnson, Allan M. Kleiman, and Susan H. McFadden. Before attending this session, I had heard of Memory Cafés but did not fully understand what they were, who they served, or how they could be integrated into library programming. By the end of the hour, I felt equipped with the knowledge and resources needed to successfully bring this type of program to my own library. The library where I work is within walking distance of two senior living apartment buildings, and our community of 16,000 is also home to several assisted living facilities. Older adults often make up the majority of attendees at our programs, so as the staff member responsible for adult programming, I attended PLA hoping to learn about meaningful services for this audience. The session began by defining the core audience for a Memory Café: people living with dementia, whether formally diagnosed or not, their caregivers, and volunteers interested in learning more. The presenters emphasized the importance of clearly communicating this audience in promotional materials. Christina M. items.title: From Skeptic to Troublemaker: One Book Club Idea That Changed My Mind
items.raw_text: I’ll admit it: library book clubs make me instantly wary. People constantly ask libraries to offer them, only to never actually show up. And a book club for kids? Forget about it. They already have plenty of assigned reading at school. So when I attended Tanvi Rastogi’s session, “Speak Up: Using Middle Grade Books to Build Allyship Muscles,” I assumed it would be a low-stakes hour to slowly wake up and drink my coffee. Friends, I didn’t even need the coffee. I left energized. Rastogi’s book club model, Good Books Young Troublemakers (GBYT), is far more than a well-intentioned idea with a catchy title. It has its own website and 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status, a sign of just how thoroughly Rastogi developed this concept after first dreaming it up in the shower. She has created a turnkey model for anyone interested in starting a chapter. Each month features a thoughtfully selected recently published title, paired with a robust downloadable discussion guide. New chapter leaders can request a starter kit complete with stickers and bookmarks mailed directly to them. Best of all, it’s free, though donations are encouraged, and there’s a pretty fun sticker if you decide to support the work. So what is GBYT all about? items.title: Renewed and Reenergized: A Rural Librarian’s PLA 2026 Experience
items.raw_text: It was a true gift to attend the recent Public Library Association Conference in Minneapolis. It had been 12 years since I last attended PLA, and I had forgotten just how exciting and energizing it can be to gather with library workers from across the country. I returned home reinvigorated, renewed, and more excited than ever to be part of our increasingly important community of librarians and information professionals. The morning keynote sessions featuring Bryan Stevenson and Dr. Ruha Benjamin were especially galvanizing. Stevenson shared how his grandmother changed his life by nurturing his love of reading, opening doors that a young boy from Alabama could scarcely have imagined. I am still reflecting on Dr. Benjamin’s perspective on AI, which she reframed, in part, as Ancestral Intelligence rather than Artificial Intelligence. The closing session with Lakota chef Sean Sherman felt especially meaningful as my library prepares to host the Americans traveling exhibit. items.title: Finding Connection and Community at PLA 2026
items.raw_text: Attending the PLA 2026 Conference in Minneapolis was an enriching experience in my professional development as a second-year MLIS student. I first learned about PLA while working as a Library Assistant and later as a Library Associate at my local public library system in Maryland. At the conference, I attended sessions on a range of topics, connected with library professionals, and shared time with fellow members of APALA. Having taken MLIS courses focused on children’s literature, multicultural resources, and the future of libraries, I was especially eager to learn more about early literacy services. In the session Intentional Early Literacy Outreach to Hispanohablantes , Andy and Carina from Arapahoe Libraries shared best practices and lessons from their efforts to connect with Spanish-speaking families. Although I am not a Spanish speaker, I appreciated the Spanish live captions throughout the presentation. One of the most valuable aspects of the session was the presenters’ candid discussion of what did not work. For example, they found that holding community meetings indoors at an apartment complex limited resident participation. Their experience highlighted the importance of time, persistence, and relationship-building with community management. They also shared a practical communications lesson: changing the language on promotional flyers to lectura gratuita , with emphasis on gratis , helped clarify that the sessions were free. items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. DeAndra Davis’s The Lovers, The Liars, And Me is a tender coming-of-age story that sensitively handles estrangement, coming out, cultural identity, and the complicated feelings that arise when you enter the adult world.
